metadata.title: Combinatorics of Linked Systems of Quartet Trees

extraction_notes.note: Abstract/Overview restatements (the quartet/quartet-tree terminology sentence and the summary of results) are not separate nodes; the formal Section 2 and theorem versions are kept.
The numerical evidence for RP1 (the $n^{3.3}$ growth) is only in Figures 2-3 (images), so only the prose assertion is extracted.
remark or example: the MaxCut behaviour on concrete linked/meshed systems is a computational observation, not a worked illustration of a definition.
Section 2 prose terminology is introduced under 'We adopt the terminology in \cite{huber}'; marked external with that citation rather than 'standard (uncited)'.

nodes.name: Taxon set [n]
nodes.statement: For any tree on a taxon set $[n]=\{1,2,\cdots, n\}$, we develop a system of quartet trees that meets B{\"o}cker’s criteria, known as a linked system.

nodes.name: Binary phylogenetic tree
nodes.statement: A \emph{binary phylogenetic tree}, $T=(V,E,\varphi)$ on a finite set of taxa $X$, is a triple consisting of a finite set of vertices, V , a set $E$ of edges between vertices, and a "labeling" map $\varphi : X \rightarrow L$, where $L \subset V$ contains all vertices of degree one or \emph{leaves}, such that the graph $(V,E)$ is an unrooted binary tree and the map $\varphi$ induces a bijection between $X$ and the set $L$ of leaves of $T$.
differentia: the graph $(V,E)$ is an unrooted binary tree
the map $\varphi$ induces a bijection between $X$ and the set $L$ of leaves of $T$
nodes.statement_short: A triple (V,E,phi) forming an unrooted binary tree whose leaves are bijectively labelled by the taxa X.

nodes.name: Exterior edge
nodes.statement: An edge that contains a leaf is an \emph{exterior edge}.

nodes.name: Internal vertex of an exterior edge
nodes.statement: The non-leaf vertex of an exterior edge is the \emph{internal vertex of $e$}, denoted $v_{int}(e)$.

nodes.name: Cherry
nodes.statement: Two exterior edges sharing an internal vertex form a \emph{cherry}.

nodes.name: Interior edge
nodes.statement: Any edge that is not an exterior edge is an \emph{interior edge}.

nodes.name: Isomorphic phylogenetic trees
nodes.statement: Phylogenetic trees, $T_1=(V_1, E_1, \varphi_1)$ and $T_2=(V_2, E_2, \varphi_2)$ on a taxon set $X$, are \emph{isomorphic} if there exists a bijective map $f : V_1 \rightarrow V_2$, called an \emph{isomorphism}, such that if $\{u,v\} \in E_1$ then $\{f (u), f (v)\} \in E_2$ and for every $x \in X$ we have $\varphi_2 (x)=f (\varphi_1 (x))$ .
nodes.statement_short: Two phylogenetic trees are isomorphic if a vertex bijection preserves edges and leaf labels.

nodes.name: Quartet tree
nodes.statement: \emph{Quartet trees} are binary phylogenetic trees on four leaves. Such trees are in one-to-one correspondence with two-element subsets of $X$ such as $\{\{a, b\},\{c,d\}\}$ according to the separation of the four leaves by the interior edge.

nodes.name: Support of a quartet tree
nodes.statement: The union of all four taxa is the \emph{support of $q$}, denoted \emph{$supp(q)$}.

nodes.name: Edge separating taxa
nodes.statement: An edge $e$ \emph{separates} taxa $a$ and $b$ from $c$ and $d$ if $\{a,b\}$ and $\{c,d\}$ are subsets of the vertex sets of different connected components of $T-\{e\}$.

nodes.name: Quartet tree displayed by a tree
nodes.statement: A quartet tree $ab|cd$ is \emph{displayed by a binary phylogenetic tree $T$} if there exists an edge $e \in E$ that separates $a$ and $b$ from $c$ and $d$.

nodes.name: Set of all quartet trees Q(X)
nodes.statement: Denote the set of all quartet trees on a taxon set $X$ by $Q(X)$.

nodes.name: System of quartet trees
nodes.statement: Any subset $Q$ of $Q(X)$ is called a \emph{system of quartet trees} on $X$ with the support defined by $supp(Q)=\displaystyle\bigcup_{q\in Q} supp(q)$.

nodes.name: Displayed quartet set Q_T
nodes.statement: Additionally, we denote the set of all quartet trees displayed by a tree $T$ by $Q_T$.

nodes.name: Compatible system of quartet trees
nodes.statement: A system of quartet trees $Q$ is \emph{compatible} if there exists a tree $T$ such that $Q \subseteq Q_T$.
differentia: there exists a tree $T$ such that $Q \subseteq Q_T$

nodes.name: Distinguished edge
nodes.statement: (\cite{semple}) Let $T = (V,E,\varphi)$ be a binary phylogenetic tree and let $ab|cd \in Q_T$. An interior edge $e$ of $T$ is \emph{distinguished} by $ab|cd$ if $e$ is the only edge that separates $a$ and $b$ from $c$ and $d$.
differentia: $e$ is the only edge that separates $a$ and $b$ from $c$ and $d$

nodes.name: Definitive system of quartet trees
nodes.statement: (\protect\cite{steel}) A system of quartet trees, $Q$, is \emph{definitive}, if up to isomorphism, there exists a unique binary phylogenetic tree $T$ for which $Q \subseteq Q_T$.
differentia: up to isomorphism, there exists a unique binary phylogenetic tree $T$ for which $Q \subseteq Q_T$

nodes.name: Böcker's criterion for definitive quartet systems
nodes.statement: (Example 3.7 of \cite{bocker1998}) If $T$ is a binary tree such that the interior edges of $T$ are labeled $E=\{e_1,...,e_{n-3}\}$, and $Q$ is a system of quartet trees such that each $q_i \in Q$ distinguishes a unique edge $e_i$ in $T$ with \[|supp(q_i)\backslash \bigcup_{j<i} supp(q_j)|= 1\] for $i=2,...,n-3$, then $Q$ is definitive.
assumptions: $T$ is a binary tree such that the interior edges of $T$ are labeled $E=\{e_1,...,e_{n-3}\}$
$Q$ is a system of quartet trees such that each $q_i \in Q$ distinguishes a unique edge $e_i$ in $T$ with \[|supp(q_i)\backslash \bigcup_{j<i} supp(q_j)|= 1\] for $i=2,...,n-3$
nodes.statement_short: If n-3 quartets each distinguish a distinct interior edge and each adds exactly one new taxon, the system is definitive.
nodes.label: bocker2

nodes.name: Associated graph G_T(Q)
nodes.statement: For a compatible system of $n-3$ quartet trees $Q$ on a taxon set $X$, define the associated graph $G_T(Q)$ with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$ as follows: \begin{itemize} \item The vertex set $V$ is the set of all quartet trees $q \in Q$ which distinguish a unique edge in $T$. \item Vertex pairs $\{q_i,q_j\}$ are connected by an edge $e \in E$ if the edge $e_i$ that $q_i$ distinguishes is adjacent to the edge $e_j$ that $q_j$ distinguishes and $|supp(\{q_i,q_j\})|=5$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Graph on quartets distinguishing unique edges; two are adjacent if their edges are adjacent and their joint support has 5 taxa.
nodes.label: order

nodes.name: Linked system
nodes.statement: Two quartet trees are \emph{linked} if their vertices are connected in $G_T(Q)$. The system of quartet trees $Q$, is \emph{a linked system} if $G_T(Q)$ is connected. See Figure \protect\ref{fig:graph} for an example.

nodes.name: Induced subtree T|Y
nodes.statement: For a binary phylogenetic tree $T$ and a subset $Y$ of $X$, let $T|Y$ denote the induced binary phylogenetic tree on leaf set $Y$ (the tree obtained from the minimal subtree connecting $Y$ by suppressing any vertices of degree $2$).

nodes.name: Quartet (four-element taxon subset)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the collection of subsets of a set $X$ of size four, we refer to all such subsets as \emph{quartets}.

nodes.name: Phylogenetic decisiveness
nodes.statement: \cite{steel} We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is \emph{phylogenetically decisive} if it satisfies the following property: If $T$ and $T$' are binary phylogenetic trees, with $T|Y=T$'$|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$, then $T=T$'.
nodes.statement_short: A collection of quartets is decisive if any two binary trees agreeing on all its quartets are equal.

nodes.name: Linked systems are definitive
nodes.statement: Every linked system of quartet trees is definitive.
assumptions: Every linked system of quartet trees
nodes.label: hierarchy

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a linked system of quartet trees on a tree $T$ on a taxon set $X$. Linked systems are of size $n-3$ and each quartet tree distinguishes a unique edge in $T$. Let $T$ be a binary phylogenetic tree on a taxon set $X$ and let $e_1$ be an interior edge adjacent to a cherry. The tree is connected, which implies we can label the remaining interior edges $\{e_2, \cdots, e_{n-3} \}$ such that $e_j$ is adjacent to some $e_i$ with $i <j$. Moreover, because the support of each pair of quartet trees $\{q_i,q_j\}$ that distinguishes adjacent edges $\{e_i,e_j\}$ is five, each pair of quartet trees shares three taxa and each additional quartet tree in $Q$ adds one new taxon to the support of $Q$. Thus, linked systems meet the criteria in Proposition \ref{bocker2} and are definitive.
nodes.statement_short: Order the interior edges outward from a cherry and check that each linked quartet adds one new taxon, so Böcker's criterion applies.

nodes.name: A definitive system that is not linked
nodes.statement: The system of quartet trees $Q=\{12|36,23|45,24|56\}$ meets the criteria established in Proposition \ref{bocker2}, and is thus definitive. The graph $G_T(Q)$ contains the three vertices $q_1$, $q_2$, and $q_3$, where $q_2$ and $q_3$ are connected by an edge and $q_1$ is an isolated vertex. Thus, $Q$ is not a linked system.
nodes.statement_short: Q={12|36,23|45,24|56} satisfies Böcker's criterion but its associated graph has an isolated vertex, so it is not linked.

nodes.name: Caterpillar
nodes.statement: (\cite{semple}) A \emph{caterpillar} on $n$ leaves is a binary phylogenetic tree for which there exists an induced subtree on a sequence of distinct interior vertices $v_1,v_2,...,v_k$ such that, for all $i \in \{1,2,...,k-1\}$, $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are adjacent.
differentia: there exists an induced subtree on a sequence of distinct interior vertices $v_1,v_2,...,v_k$ such that, for all $i \in \{1,2,...,k-1\}$, $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}$ are adjacent

nodes.name: Edge ordering of a caterpillar
nodes.statement: The ordering of vertices in a caterpillar tree induces an ordering of interior edges $e_i$ where $e_i$ connects $v_i$ with $v_{i+1}$.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the decisiveness threshold k(n)
nodes.statement: The minimal number $k(n)$ such that every collection of quartets $S$ with $|S| \geq k$ is decisive is greater than ${n \choose 4} - (n-3)$.
conclusions: The minimal number $k(n)$ such that every collection of quartets $S$ with $|S| \geq k$ is decisive is greater than ${n \choose 4} - (n-3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Some collection of C(n,4)-(n-3) quartets is not decisive, so k(n) exceeds that size.
nodes.label: ge

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.3
nodes.statement: Let \{a,b,c\} be a subset of $X$. We define $T_1$, $T_2$, and $T_3$ to be three distinct caterpillar trees of size $n \geq 4$ that differ only in the placement of three taxa $a$, $b$, and $c$, such that for each tree $v_{int}(a), v_{int}(b)$ and $v_{int}(c)$ are incident to $e_1$. Denote $\mathcal{S}$ the set of $n-3$ sets $\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{n-3}Y_i=\{a,b,c,y|y \in X-\{a,b,c\}\}$ and let $\mathcal{S'}$ be the complement of $\mathcal{S}$. We observe that for all $Y\in \mathcal{S'}$ we have $T_1|Y=T_2|Y=T_3|Y$, but $T_1 \neq T_2 \neq T_3$. Therefore, $S'$ is not decisive. Since $|\mathcal{S'}|={n \choose 4} - (n-3)$ the minimal number $k(n)$ such that every collection $\mathcal{S}$ of quartets with $|\mathcal{S}| \geq k$ is decisive is greater than ${n \choose 4} - (n-3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct three caterpillars differing only in taxa a,b,c near e_1; they agree on every quartet outside the n-3 sets containing a,b,c.

nodes.name: Taxon partition induced by an interior edge
nodes.statement: In a phylogenetic tree, each interior edge $e=(v_l,v_r)$ is adjacent to four edges $e_i$, $e_j$, $e_h$, and $e_k$, which divide the tree into four components and partition the set of taxa $X$ into four distinct sets $A_i$, $A_j$, $A_k$, and $A_h$ with $x \in A_n$ if the unique path from $x$ to $v_l$ contains the edge $e_n$.
nodes.statement_short: An interior edge's four adjacent edges split the taxa into four sets A_i, A_j, A_k, A_h.

nodes.name: Quartet tree substitution
nodes.statement: Let $q=ij|kh$ be a quartet tree that distinguishes an edge $e$ and let $i \in A_i$, $j \in A_j$, $k \in A_k$, and $h \in A_h$, where $A_i$, $A_j$, $A_k$, and $A_h$ are partitions of $X$ induced by $e$. For $x\in X - supp(q)$ define the \emph{quartet tree substitution} $q(x)$ to be the unique quartet tree in which the taxon $x \in A_n$ replaces the taxon in $q$ that is in $supp(q) \cap A_n$.
nodes.statement_short: q(x) replaces the taxon of q lying in the same edge-induced block as x by x.

nodes.name: Substituted quartet distinguishes the same edge
nodes.statement: Notice $q(x)$ and $q$ must distinguish the same edge of the tree.
conclusions: $q(x)$ and $q$ must distinguish the same edge of the tree

nodes.name: Vine of a quartet tree
nodes.statement: Let the quartet tree $q$ distinguish an edge $e$ of a tree. Define the \emph{vine of q} by $v(q)=\{q\} \cup \displaystyle\bigcup_{x\in X-supp(q)}q(x)$. We refer to $q$ as the \emph{seed} of the vine.
nodes.statement_short: The vine of q is q together with all its substitutions q(x) for taxa x outside supp(q); q is its seed.

nodes.name: Linked vines
nodes.statement: Two vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ are \emph{linked} if for each $q_i \in v(q_i)$ there exists a unique $q_j \in v(q_j)$ such that $q_i$ and $q_j$ are linked.

nodes.name: Linked quartets have linked vines
nodes.statement: If $q_i$ and $q_j$ are linked quartet trees, then the associated vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ are linked.
conclusions: the associated vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ are linked
nodes.label: linkedquartets

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.7
nodes.statement: Assume that $\{q_i,q_j\}$ are the seeds of the adjacent edges $e_i$ and $e_j$ and are linked in $T$. Let $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ be the associated vines. Because the $supp(q_i,q_j)=5$, each quartet tree contains one taxon that the other does not. Let $z$ be the taxon in $supp(q_j)-supp(q_i)$ and $y$ be the taxon in $supp(q_i)-supp(q_j)$. Use quartet tree substitution to construct the quartet trees $q_i(z)$ and $q_j(y)$. By construction, $supp(q_i,q_j)=supp(q_i(z),q_j(y))$ and $q_i(z)$ and $q_j(y)$ are linked. Use quartet tree substitution with each remaining taxon $x \in X-supp(q_i,q_j)$ on $q_i$ and $q_j$ to construct the remaining quartet trees in $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$. In the construction of each $\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\}$ one taxon (Case 1) or two taxa (Case 2) are removed and one taxon $x$ is introduced. Thus, for $x \in X - (supp(q_i,q_j))$ we have $4 \leq |supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \leq 6$. In Case 1, $x$ replaces the same taxon in $q_i$ and $q_j$ and $supp(q_i,q_j)$ remains the same. In Case 2, $x$ replaces one taxon in $q_i$ and a different taxon in $q_j$. Assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=4$ and $q_i(x)=q_j(x)$. This is not possible since $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish different edges. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 4$. Now assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=6$. Recall that $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish the edges $e_i$ and $e_j$. Thus, in order for $x$ to replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$, $x$ would have to be in two different sets of the partition that $e_i$ induces on $X$. This is not possible because $x$ cannot be in two different sets of a partition. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 6$. Thus, in this case, $x$ replaces one taxon in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and one taxon in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\})|=5$. Therefore the vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ are linked.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute each remaining taxon into both seeds and case on whether it replaces one or two taxa. Ruling out joint supports of size 4 and 6 leaves size 5, so substituted pairs are linked.

nodes.name: Meshed system
nodes.statement: A \emph{meshed system} on a tree $T$ with taxon set $X$ is an $(n-3)$ by $(n-3)$ array of quartet trees, where each row is a linked system and each column is a vine.
differentia: each row is a linked system

nodes.name: Meshed systems survive removal of n-4 quartet trees
nodes.statement: Note that the existence of a meshed system ensures that the removal of up to $n-4$ quartet trees from $Q_T$ must leave at least one definitive set.
assumptions: the existence of a meshed system
conclusions: the removal of up to $n-4$ quartet trees from $Q_T$ must leave at least one definitive set

nodes.name: Existence of meshed systems
nodes.statement: For any binary phylogenetic tree $T$ on a taxon set $X$, the system $Q_T$ of all quartet trees displayed by $T$ contains a meshed system.
assumptions: any binary phylogenetic tree $T$ on a taxon set $X$
conclusions: the system $Q_T$ of all quartet trees displayed by $T$ contains a meshed system
nodes.label: number

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.9
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a binary phylogenetic tree on a taxon set $X$ and let $e_1$ be an interior edge adjacent to a cherry. The tree is connected, which implies we can label the remaining interior edges $\{e_2, \cdots, e_{n-3} \}$ such that $e_j$ is adjacent to some $e_i$ with $i <j$. Let $e_j$ be adjacent to $e_i$ with $i<j$. We know that $e_i$ separates $T$ into two connected components $T_i^a$ and $T_i^b$. Moreover, $e_j$ separates $T$ into two connected components $T_j^a$ and $T_j^b$. Because $e_i$ and $e_j$ are adjacent, $supp(T_i^b) \cap supp(T_j^a) \neq \emptyset$. Let $q_i=ab|cd$ and $q_j=ac|de$ such that $a \in supp(T_i^a)$, $c \in supp(T_j^b)$, and $d \in supp(T_i^b) \cap supp(T_j^a)$. Thus, $q_i$ and $q_j$ are linked for all $e_i$ and $e_j$ in $T$. Thus, we have a linked system that makes up the first row of our matrix. Using quartet tree substitution, construct vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$. By Theorem \ref{linkedquartets} the vines $v(q_j)$ and $v(q_i)$ are linked. Thus, we have $n-3$ disjoint columns of quartet trees in our matrix. Additionally, for each pair of linked quartet trees $\{q_i,q_j\}$ in row one, there exists a pair $\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\}$ in the remaining rows of the matrix that are linked. Thus, we have $n-3$ rows of linked systems. Therefore, $Q_T$ contains a meshed system.
nodes.statement_short: Build a linked first row by ordering edges outward from a cherry, then extend each seed to its vine; Theorem 3.7 makes every row linked.

nodes.name: Optimal decisiveness threshold k(n)
nodes.statement: The number $k(n)={n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ is the smallest number such that every collection of quartets $\mathcal{S}$ on a taxon set $X=[n]$ such that $\mathcal{S} \geq k$ is decisive.
assumptions: every collection of quartets $\mathcal{S}$ on a taxon set $X=[n]$ such that $\mathcal{S} \geq k$
conclusions: The number $k(n)={n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ is the smallest number such that every collection of quartets $\mathcal{S}$ on a taxon set $X=[n]$ such that $\mathcal{S} \geq k$ is decisive.
nodes.statement_short: Every collection of at least C(n,4)-(n-4) quartets is decisive, and this threshold is optimal.
nodes.label: thm:big

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.10
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a collection of quartets on a taxon set $X=[n]$, with $|\mathcal{S}| \ge {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$. Let $T$ and $T'$ be two phylogenetic trees such that $T|Y=T$'$|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. We define $Q \subset Q_T$ to be the collection of $T|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. By Theorem \ref{number}, $Q_T$ contains a meshed system $M$. By the pigeon hole principle, if $|Q| \geq {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ then $Q$ must contain one of the linked systems in $M$, and by Theorem \ref{hierarchy}, $Q$ is definitive. Thus, $T$ is the unique tree which displays $Q$. However since $Q$ is also $T'|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$, we must have $T=T'$. Therefore, $\mathcal{S}$ is decisive. Moreover, Theorem \ref{ge} shows that $k \geq {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$. Therefore $k(n)={n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ is the minimal number such that every collection of quartets with $|\mathcal{S}| \geq k$ is decisive.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole on the n-3 disjoint linked systems of a meshed system leaves a linked, hence definitive, subsystem; optimality from Theorem 3.3.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the probability of decisiveness
nodes.statement: The probability $p(X,k)$ that an arbitrary collection of $k$ quartets is decisive has the property \[p(X,k) \geq \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n-3} (-1)^{i+1}{{n-3} \choose i}{{|Q_T|-i(n-3)} \choose {|Q_T|-k}}}{{|Q_T| \choose {k}}}.\]
conclusions: The probability $p(X,k)$ that an arbitrary collection of $k$ quartets is decisive has the property \[p(X,k) \geq \frac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n-3} (-1)^{i+1}{{n-3} \choose i}{{|Q_T|-i(n-3)} \choose {|Q_T|-k}}}{{|Q_T| \choose {k}}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion-exclusion lower bound on the probability that k random quartets are decisive.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.11
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a collection of $k$ quartets. Let $T$ and $T'$ be two phylogenetic trees such that $T|Y=T'|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. We define $Q \subset Q_T$ to be the collection of $T|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. Following Theorem \protect\ref{thm:big}, if $Q$ contains a definitive set of quartet trees, then $S$ is decisive. By Theorem \protect\ref{hierarchy}, if a collection of compatible quartet trees contains a linked system of quartets, then it is definitive. Thus, the probability that a collection $\mathcal{S}$ is decisive is at least the probability that $Q$ contains one of the $n-3$ disjoint linked systems constructed in Theorem \protect\ref{number}. The formula follows from applying the inclusion-exclusion principle to count the number of subsets of size $k$, which contain one of the disjoint systems of linked quartets.
nodes.statement_short: Decisiveness is implied by containing one of the n-3 disjoint linked systems of a meshed system; count such k-subsets by inclusion-exclusion.

nodes.name: Empirical growth n^3.3 of quartets needed for decisiveness
nodes.statement: Notice the number of quartets needed to ensure the sample is decisive with accuracy of $25 \%$ is on the order of $n^c$ with $c \sim 3.3$ and is almost indistinguishable from the number required to ensure $99\%$ accuracy.
nodes.statement_short: Numerically, the quartets needed for decisiveness with 25% or 99% probability both scale like n^3.3.

nodes.name: Quartets MaxCut on linked versus meshed systems
nodes.statement: However, some supertree methods such as Quartets MaxCut do not always return a fully resolved tree even when the input sets contain small definitive systems. For example, MaxCut does not return a fully resolved tree for the linked system $Q_1=\{12|35,13|45,14|56\}$, but returns the correct tree for the meshed system $M=\{Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\}$ where $Q_2=\{12|34,23|45,24|56\}$ and $Q_3=\{12|36,23|46,34|56\}$.
nodes.statement_short: MaxCut fails to fully resolve a small linked system but recovers the tree from a meshed system.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $Q$ be a linked system of quartet trees on a tree $T$ on a taxon set $X$. Linked systems are of size $n-3$ and each quartet tree distinguishes a unique edge in $T$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a linked system Q on T and recall its properties.

nodes.name: Edge ordering
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a binary phylogenetic tree on a taxon set $X$ and let $e_1$ be an interior edge adjacent to a cherry. The tree is connected, which implies we can label the remaining interior edges $\{e_2, \cdots, e_{n-3} \}$ such that $e_j$ is adjacent to some $e_i$ with $i <j$.
nodes.statement_short: Order interior edges outward from a cherry-adjacent edge $e_1$.

nodes.name: One new taxon per quartet
nodes.statement: Moreover, because the support of each pair of quartet trees $\{q_i,q_j\}$ that distinguishes adjacent edges $\{e_i,e_j\}$ is five, each pair of quartet trees shares three taxa and each additional quartet tree in $Q$ adds one new taxon to the support of $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Each successive quartet adds exactly one new taxon.

nodes.name: Conclude via Böcker
nodes.statement: Thus, linked systems meet the criteria in Proposition \ref{bocker2} and are definitive.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Böcker's criterion (Proposition 2.5).

nodes.name: Three caterpillars
nodes.statement: Let \{a,b,c\} be a subset of $X$. We define $T_1$, $T_2$, and $T_3$ to be three distinct caterpillar trees of size $n \geq 4$ that differ only in the placement of three taxa $a$, $b$, and $c$, such that for each tree $v_{int}(a), v_{int}(b)$ and $v_{int}(c)$ are incident to $e_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct three caterpillars differing only in placement of a,b,c.

nodes.name: Agreement on complement
nodes.statement: Denote $\mathcal{S}$ the set of $n-3$ sets $\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^{n-3}Y_i=\{a,b,c,y|y \in X-\{a,b,c\}\}$ and let $\mathcal{S'}$ be the complement of $\mathcal{S}$. We observe that for all $Y\in \mathcal{S'}$ we have $T_1|Y=T_2|Y=T_3|Y$, but $T_1 \neq T_2 \neq T_3$.
nodes.statement_short: Trees agree on every quartet outside the n-3 sets containing a,b,c.

nodes.name: Complement not decisive
nodes.statement: Therefore, $S'$ is not decisive.
nodes.statement_short: So the complement collection is not decisive.

nodes.name: Conclude bound
nodes.statement: Since $|\mathcal{S'}|={n \choose 4} - (n-3)$ the minimal number $k(n)$ such that every collection $\mathcal{S}$ of quartets with $|\mathcal{S}| \geq k$ is decisive is greater than ${n \choose 4} - (n-3)$.
nodes.statement_short: Count the complement to bound k(n).

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Assume that $\{q_i,q_j\}$ are the seeds of the adjacent edges $e_i$ and $e_j$ and are linked in $T$. Let $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ be the associated vines.
nodes.statement_short: Take linked seeds of adjacent edges and their vines.

nodes.name: Swap distinct taxa
nodes.statement: Because the $supp(q_i,q_j)=5$, each quartet tree contains one taxon that the other does not. Let $z$ be the taxon in $supp(q_j)-supp(q_i)$ and $y$ be the taxon in $supp(q_i)-supp(q_j)$. Use quartet tree substitution to construct the quartet trees $q_i(z)$ and $q_j(y)$. By construction, $supp(q_i,q_j)=supp(q_i(z),q_j(y))$ and $q_i(z)$ and $q_j(y)$ are linked.
nodes.statement_short: Swap the two non-shared taxa to get a linked pair $q_i(z),q_j(y)$.

nodes.name: Support range
nodes.statement: Use quartet tree substitution with each remaining taxon $x \in X-supp(q_i,q_j)$ on $q_i$ and $q_j$ to construct the remaining quartet trees in $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$. In the construction of each $\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\}$ one taxon (Case 1) or two taxa (Case 2) are removed and one taxon $x$ is introduced. Thus, for $x \in X - (supp(q_i,q_j))$ we have $4 \leq |supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \leq 6$.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting any other taxon gives joint support between 4 and 6.

nodes.name: Case 1
nodes.statement: In Case 1, $x$ replaces the same taxon in $q_i$ and $q_j$ and $supp(q_i,q_j)$ remains the same.
nodes.statement_short: Case 1: x replaces the same taxon; support unchanged.

nodes.name: Case 2
nodes.statement: In Case 2, $x$ replaces one taxon in $q_i$ and a different taxon in $q_j$. Assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=4$ and $q_i(x)=q_j(x)$. This is not possible since $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish different edges. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 4$. Now assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=6$. Recall that $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish the edges $e_i$ and $e_j$. Thus, in order for $x$ to replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$, $x$ would have to be in two different sets of the partition that $e_i$ induces on $X$. This is not possible because $x$ cannot be in two different sets of a partition. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 6$. Thus, in this case, $x$ replaces one taxon in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and one taxon in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\})|=5$.
nodes.statement_short: Case 2: x replaces different taxa; joint support must be 5.

nodes.name: Subcase support 4
nodes.statement: Assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=4$ and $q_i(x)=q_j(x)$. This is not possible since $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish different edges. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 4$.
nodes.statement_short: Support 4 would force equal quartets on different edges; impossible.

nodes.name: Subcase support 6
nodes.statement: Now assume that $x$ replaces two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$. Then, $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))|=6$. Recall that $q_i$ and $q_j$ distinguish the edges $e_i$ and $e_j$. Thus, in order for $x$ to replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$, $x$ would have to be in two different sets of the partition that $e_i$ induces on $X$. This is not possible because $x$ cannot be in two different sets of a partition. Thus, $x$ does not replace two different taxa in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(q_i(x),q_j(x))| \neq 6$.
nodes.statement_short: Support 6 would put x in two partition blocks; impossible.

nodes.name: Support is 5
nodes.statement: Thus, in this case, $x$ replaces one taxon in $supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and one taxon in $supp(q_i,q_j)-supp(q_i \cap q_j)$ and $|supp(\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\})|=5$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence joint support is 5 in Case 2.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore the vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$ are linked.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude the vines are linked.

nodes.name: Edge ordering
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be a binary phylogenetic tree on a taxon set $X$ and let $e_1$ be an interior edge adjacent to a cherry. The tree is connected, which implies we can label the remaining interior edges $\{e_2, \cdots, e_{n-3} \}$ such that $e_j$ is adjacent to some $e_i$ with $i <j$.
nodes.statement_short: Order interior edges outward from a cherry-adjacent edge.

nodes.name: First row
nodes.statement: Let $e_j$ be adjacent to $e_i$ with $i<j$. We know that $e_i$ separates $T$ into two connected components $T_i^a$ and $T_i^b$. Moreover, $e_j$ separates $T$ into two connected components $T_j^a$ and $T_j^b$. Because $e_i$ and $e_j$ are adjacent, $supp(T_i^b) \cap supp(T_j^a) \neq \emptyset$. Let $q_i=ab|cd$ and $q_j=ac|de$ such that $a \in supp(T_i^a)$, $c \in supp(T_j^b)$, and $d \in supp(T_i^b) \cap supp(T_j^a)$. Thus, $q_i$ and $q_j$ are linked for all $e_i$ and $e_j$ in $T$. Thus, we have a linked system that makes up the first row of our matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Choose linked seeds for adjacent edges, forming a linked first row.

nodes.name: Columns via vines
nodes.statement: Using quartet tree substitution, construct vines $v(q_i)$ and $v(q_j)$. By Theorem \ref{linkedquartets} the vines $v(q_j)$ and $v(q_i)$ are linked. Thus, we have $n-3$ disjoint columns of quartet trees in our matrix. Additionally, for each pair of linked quartet trees $\{q_i,q_j\}$ in row one, there exists a pair $\{q_i(x),q_j(x)\}$ in the remaining rows of the matrix that are linked. Thus, we have $n-3$ rows of linked systems.
nodes.statement_short: Extend seeds to vines; Theorem 3.7 links them, giving n-3 linked rows.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore, $Q_T$ contains a meshed system.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude Q_T contains a meshed system.

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a collection of quartets on a taxon set $X=[n]$, with $|\mathcal{S}| \ge {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$. Let $T$ and $T'$ be two phylogenetic trees such that $T|Y=T$'$|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. We define $Q \subset Q_T$ to be the collection of $T|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix S, two trees agreeing on S, and the induced quartet trees Q.

nodes.name: Meshed system exists
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{number}, $Q_T$ contains a meshed system $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Q_T contains a meshed system (Theorem 3.9).

nodes.name: Pigeonhole
nodes.statement: By the pigeon hole principle, if $|Q| \geq {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ then $Q$ must contain one of the linked systems in $M$, and by Theorem \ref{hierarchy}, $Q$ is definitive.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole: Q contains a linked row, hence is definitive (Theorem 3.1).

nodes.name: S is decisive
nodes.statement: Thus, $T$ is the unique tree which displays $Q$. However since $Q$ is also $T'|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$, we must have $T=T'$. Therefore, $\mathcal{S}$ is decisive.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness forces T=T', so S is decisive.

nodes.name: Optimality
nodes.statement: Moreover, Theorem \ref{ge} shows that $k \geq {n \choose 4} - (n-4)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound from Theorem 3.3.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $k(n)={n \choose 4} - (n-4)$ is the minimal number such that every collection of quartets with $|\mathcal{S}| \geq k$ is decisive.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude k(n)=C(n,4)-(n-4).

nodes.name: Setup
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a collection of $k$ quartets. Let $T$ and $T'$ be two phylogenetic trees such that $T|Y=T'|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$. We define $Q \subset Q_T$ to be the collection of $T|Y$ for all $Y \in \mathcal{S}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix S of size k, two agreeing trees, and induced quartet trees Q.

nodes.name: Definitive implies decisive
nodes.statement: Following Theorem \protect\ref{thm:big}, if $Q$ contains a definitive set of quartet trees, then $S$ is decisive.
nodes.statement_short: A definitive subset of Q makes S decisive.

nodes.name: Linked implies definitive
nodes.statement: By Theorem \protect\ref{hierarchy}, if a collection of compatible quartet trees contains a linked system of quartets, then it is definitive.
nodes.statement_short: Containing a linked system implies definitive (Theorem 3.1).

nodes.name: Reduce to containment
nodes.statement: Thus, the probability that a collection $\mathcal{S}$ is decisive is at least the probability that $Q$ contains one of the $n-3$ disjoint linked systems constructed in Theorem \protect\ref{number}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound probability by that of containing one of the n-3 disjoint linked rows.

nodes.name: Inclusion-exclusion
nodes.statement: The formula follows from applying the inclusion-exclusion principle to count the number of subsets of size $k$, which contain one of the disjoint systems of linked quartets.
nodes.statement_short: Count via inclusion-exclusion.
